title: Social media and the tongue
hookLine: the adab of speech applies online too

lines: DOES IT COUNT IF YOU TYPE IT?
WORDS ONCE HAD A FACE IN FRONT OF THEM.
cards: Does backbiting count if you type it instead of saying it? Does passing on a rumor count if all you did was tap share? Does a cruel comment under a stranger's photo count, if the stranger never reads it?

The sayings about speech come from a world of rooms, doorways and roads, where a listener usually stood in front of the speaker. Now a word can reach a crowd of screens before its writer has put the phone down.
Today takes the old manners of the tongue, what Muslims call adab, and carries them online.

teach.b: Start with the plainest rule. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say what is good, or keep silent. Good, or nothing.
There's no third box marked technically true but unkind. Then a second report, also in al-Bukhari: a Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand other Muslims are safe.

teach.h: THE TONGUE AND THE HAND, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: Tongue and hand, side by side. On a phone, the hand does the talking. The thumbs are the tongue.
Third, the rumor. Imam Muslim, in the introduction to his collection, keeps a saying that it is enough of a lie for a person to pass on everything he hears. Not inventing anything.

And the Qur'an, in the chapter called The Private Apartments, asks the believers to check a report brought by someone untrustworthy before acting on it, so they don't harm people in ignorance and regret it afterward.
A few verses later, the same chapter forbids backbiting, and asks, in a picture that's hard to forget, whether any of you would love to eat the flesh of a dead brother. Hold the four up to a screen.
Say good or stay quiet. Let your hand be as safe as your tongue.

teach.h: DON'T PASS ON EVERYTHING YOU HEAR.
teach.b: Don't pass on everything that reaches you.
Check it before you act on it.
None of these rules mentions a phone, and every one of them fits on one.

how: Some Muslim teachers apply the hadith on speech, say good or keep silent, to messaging and social media, and some Muslims make a habit of checking a story before they share it.

games.q: what does “social media and the tongue” mean?
o: a ruling that Muslims should stay off social media
online speech, which the old rules about talk don't cover
the old manners of speech, carried into every post and share

games.q: the manners of the tongue — tap the pairs.
p: others should be safe from both
enough of a lie, says the report

s: the hadith gives three choices: good, true, or silent
it gives two: say what is good, or keep silent.
a report in Muslim's introduction warns against passing on everything you hear
it calls that enough of a lie, even when you invented nothing.
the Qur'an asks believers to check a report before acting on it
in the chapter called The Private Apartments (49:6), so as not to harm people in ignorance.

games.q: a dramatic story about someone you know is going around your group chat. you can't tell if it's true. what fits the saying in Muslim's introduction and 49:6?
o: share it with "not sure if this is true" on top.
pass it on to just a few close friends.
pass on nothing until you know it's true.
games.why: the saying calls it enough of a lie to pass on everything you hear, and 49:6 asks for checking first. a disclaimer or a small audience is still passing it on.

practice: Think back over the last few things you typed to anyone, a message, a comment, a post, and let them come up one at a time without judging. For each, ask the hadith's question: was it good, or would silence have been better?
If one stings a little, notice it and let it go with the breath; if you pray, you can ask for a careful tongue.

wordCard.voice: Social media and the tongue. The old manners of speech, say good or stay silent, check before you pass it on, carried into every post and comment. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the tongue, and also a language or a way of speaking.

carryVoice: Your line: the tongue has thumbs. A week that began with scholars saying no ends, like much of it, with words. See you tomorrow.
